source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school math problems (GSM-IC) makes models fail on problems they solved. Distractors that share roles or numbers with the question hurt most.
numbers: No more than 18% of originally solved problems stay solved across all distractor types. Macro accuracy under 30% for text-davinci-003 and code-davinci-002 with all prompts. Role-overlap distractors push text-davinci-003 macro accuracy to 0 on some problem types.
limits: GPT-3 family models; arithmetic only, not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant but topical text is a surface cue that pulls the model off the task. Input hygiene (S1) should strip or flag details that do not enter the answer.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context (mitigations)
finding: Self-consistency, distractor-containing exemplars and an explicit instruction to ignore irrelevant information each helped, but none closed the gap.
numbers: Self-consistency with 20 samples: correct answer present in 99.7% of problems; 0-CoT micro accuracy gain 35.5 points; yet best macro accuracy over all prompts only 45%. Instructed prompting improves CoT, LTM and Program prompts consistently.
limits: Presence of the right answer in 20 samples is recall, not accuracy; a selector is still needed.
agent_relevance: Matches G4/G5: samples contain the right answer but one model's vote is not proof. An explicit 'some facts may be irrelevant' line is a cheap measured aid.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025, ICLR) GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Rewriting GSM8K problems with new names and numbers shifts accuracy and raises variance. Name changes matter little, number changes more, extra clauses most.
numbers: Gap between GSM8K and the GSM-Symbolic distribution differs by model (for example Gemma2-9B shows a visible gap); variance rises from names to numbers to added clauses (P1, P2). Exact per-model values read from figures only.
limits: The authors' reading (pattern matching rather than reasoning) is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Surface variation changes outputs, so test the answer under a restated version of the problem (the held-out or mutated-input check, G3).

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025, ICLR) GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs (GSM-NoOp)
finding: One seemingly relevant but inconsequential clause (No-Op) causes large drops. Models convert cue words such as 'discount' into an operation such as multiplication regardless of context.
numbers: Drops up to 65% (Phi-3-mini over 65%); o1-preview and other strong models also decline significantly. Eight shots of the same question did not recover performance (within standard deviation).
quote: models tend to convert statements to operations without truly understanding their meaning
limits: Fixed 8-shot setup; no test of an explicit 'ignore irrelevant' instruction.
agent_relevance: A direct LLM analogue of keyword-to-action symptom matching. Demonstration alone did not fix it.

source: McCoy et al. (2019) Right for the Wrong Reasons: Diagnosing Syntactic Heuristics in NLI (HANS)
finding: Models trained on MNLI score high but use three shallow rules: lexical overlap implies entailment, subsequence implies entailment, constituent implies entailment. HANS breaks these rules on purpose.
numbers: BERT, ESIM, DA and SPINN all predict entailment nearly always on HANS: near-perfect when entailment is true, near-zero when not. BERT lexical-overlap subcases: 39% on conjunction, 0% on subject/object swap; 49% on a conditional-clause subcase.
limits: 2019 models; larger later models do better, but the principle (test where cue and truth disagree) stands.
agent_relevance: The machine version of rule-based behaviour in Rasmussen's scheme: works on typical cases, fails on atypical ones. Build checks where cue and truth disagree.

source: McCoy et al. (2023/2024) Embers of Autoregression
finding: LLM accuracy depends on how probable the task and the output are, even for deterministic tasks. Common cases are solved, rare variants are not.
numbers: GPT-4 decoding a simple cipher: 51% when the output is a high-probability word sequence, 13% when low probability. Eleven tasks, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
limits: Artificial tasks; effect sizes vary by task.
agent_relevance: Pattern frequency plays the role of familiarity in human fast diagnosis. Rare faults are the likely blind spot, so add checks when the case is unusual.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual tasks
finding: On 11 tasks, GPT-4 and others do well on default versions but drop on counterfactual versions with the same logic and changed conventions (base-9 arithmetic, 1-based indexing, altered word order).
numbers: Performance 'substantially and consistently degrades' on counterfactuals yet stays above chance. GPT-3.5 parseable programs fall from 99% to 62%, 71% and 75% under flipped or rotated drawing settings.
limits: Counterfactual forms may be both rarer and harder to state; authors still read the gap as narrow procedures.
agent_relevance: Surface matching to a familiar setup. State the nonstandard conditions and check with a worked example under them.

source: Wu et al. (2024) counterfactual: CoT and few-shot
finding: Zero-shot CoT and demonstrations did not remove the counterfactual gap; in two bases 1-shot was worse than 0-shot.
numbers: Footnote 10: bases 11 and 16 suffer from 1-shot demonstration relative to 0-shot (guess: letter digits).
limits: Hypothesis only.
agent_relevance: Examples can themselves add a misleading surface cue.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using Counterfactual Tasks to Evaluate the Generality of Analogical Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Boundary test of Webb et al.'s claim that GPT-3 solves letter-string analogies. With permuted or symbol alphabets GPT models decline sharply while humans stay high.
numbers: Humans high on original and counterfactual problems; GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 all degrade on counterfactual. Error type 'alternate rule': GPT-3 5.81%, GPT-4 22%, GPT-3.5 38.59%.
limits: Small human sample; Webb and colleagues contest parts of it (not read here).
agent_relevance: Matching to seen surface forms rather than structure. Relevant to case-retrieval style diagnosis.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: On NLI, syllogisms and Wason selection, models and humans both do better when meaning supports the logically correct answer. Belief and logic are mixed in both.
numbers: Paper cites Evans et al.: people called invalid syllogisms valid 90% of the time when the conclusion was believable. Models show the same direction of effect across the three task families; per-model percentages not recorded.
quote: humans reason more reliably when the semantic content of a problem supports the correct logical inferences
limits: Parallel answer patterns do not prove the same mechanism.
agent_relevance: A plausible story gets accepted. Test the claim in abstract form too.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024), Wason selection task part
finding: On Wason the models and humans score lower than on NLI or syllogisms and depend strongly on content (realistic vs arbitrary vs nonsense).
numbers: Bootstrap 95% CIs reported; cited work: graduate mathematics majors and mathematicians under 50% on the arbitrary Wason task.
limits: No per-model numbers extracted.
agent_relevance: Abstract rule tasks are hard; realistic cover helps by cue, not by rule.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Biasing features in the prompt (answer is always A; a suggested answer) shift answers, and CoT text does not mention the cue. The explanation is a rationalisation.
numbers: Accuracy drops up to 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks. Zero-shot CoT Suggested Answer: -36.3% GPT-3.5, -30.6% Claude 1.0; few-shot CoT: -24.1% and -21.5%. Answer-is-always-A: -18.7% GPT-3.5, -4.7% Claude 1.0.
limits: Older models; synthetic cues.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 (written reasoning is no record of cause). A hypothesis stated in a report or by a user is a cue the model follows.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) CoT effect on bias sensitivity
finding: CoT reduced sensitivity to some biases, not others.
numbers: Answer-is-always-A: CoT weakly decreases sensitivity for GPT-3.5 (55.2 to 58.7%) but a lot for Claude 1.0 (63.2 to 80.1%); numbers as printed in text.
limits: Arrow direction lost in extraction; read with care.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on CoT as a cue filter.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors
finding: Models prefer certain option labels (selection bias), mostly a token-prior effect rather than position.
numbers: 1,000 MMLU items with 250 correct answers per letter: llama-30B chose A/B/C/D 34.6/27.3/22.3/15.8% of the time. Debiasing (PriDe) estimates the prior on about 5% of samples and applies it to the rest, label-free.
limits: Multiple-choice only.
agent_relevance: Code can remove this surface preference: shuffle options and aggregate in code (G5).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with LLMs
finding: Reordering premises of a logically identical problem changes accuracy. Models prefer the order that matches the proof order.
numbers: Drops of over 30%; GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L fall 20-30%; some models fall from above 65% to below 25% on one setting; R-GSM benchmark also shows significant drops.
limits: Deductive and math tasks.
agent_relevance: Presentation order is a surface cue. Restate the problem in canonical order in S1.

source: Tang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Lazy Learners: Shortcuts in In-Context Learning
finding: Trigger words inserted in in-context examples work as shortcuts; larger models rely on them more.
numbers: GPT2-large with a common-word shortcut: MR accuracy 63.46% to 22.01% (-41.45%), below chance. Average drop for GPT2-large over three datasets 33.71% vs 1.04% for GPT2-base.
limits: Small older models (GPT-2, OPT).
agent_relevance: A chance feature in the examples becomes the diagnosis. Check examples for accidental label correlates.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: On 1,273 USMLE questions with seven cognitive-bias phrases added, every model lost accuracy. False consensus hurt most, confirmation least.
numbers: No-bias accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral-8x7B 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama-13B 33.4%. Mean drop over models: false consensus 24.9%, frequency 18.2%, recency 12.9%, confirmation 8.1%. GPT-4 worst case -14.0% (false consensus), confirmation -0.2%. GPT-3.5 mean -37.4%.
limits: Bias injected as simple sentences; exam questions, not patients.
agent_relevance: Anchoring-style cues work on models too. Crowd-opinion statements in an input are a hazard.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) BiasMedQA mitigation
finding: Warning about bias or showing bias examples helped GPT-4 but gave little to weaker models.
numbers: GPT-4 frequency bias accuracy 0.627 to 0.720 with bias education; recency 0.679 to 0.742 with one-shot negative example. Mixtral and GPT-3.5 only marginal gains. PaLM-2 refused 94.4% (one-shot) and 99.5% (few-shot) of queries via safety filters.
limits: Small model range.
agent_relevance: A generic debias line is not enough for weak models; detect in code.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: Prompting GPT-4 to reason intuitively, analytically, by differential or Bayesian method on MedQA does not change accuracy vs plain CoT; GPT-3.5 gets worse with the harder styles.
numbers: GPT-4 (N=497): CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, differential 78%, analytic 78%, Bayesian 72% (-3.4%, P=0.07). GPT-3.5: differential 38% (-8%, P<0.001), Bayesian 42% (-4%, P=0.02).
limits: Multiple-choice exam items.
agent_relevance: Forcing slow analytic style gains nothing here (G1): doubt must come from a signal.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based Agents for Root Cause Analysis
finding: A ReAct agent with retrieval tools tested on real Microsoft production incidents performs competitively with strong retrieval and CoT baselines on text metrics but with much higher factual accuracy.
numbers: Table 2 C-BLEU: CoT 6.31, retrieval baseline k=10 5.97, ReAct BR 5.53, ReAct S+Q BM25 5.59, IR-CoT ST 3.91. Other columns garbled and not used.
limits: Single company dataset; text-overlap metrics.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of similar past incidents is surface-similarity matching; tool calls that fetch fresh logs counter it.

source: Wang et al. (2023) RCAgent: Cloud Root Cause Analysis by Autonomous Agents with Tool-Augmented LLMs
finding: An agent loop with tools, self-consistency over trajectories and stored observations keeps cloud RCA stable.
numbers: Full system 99.38% pass rate within 15 steps, 7.93% invalid rate; removing observation key-value storage cut pass rate 33.54% with 70.95% invalid rate; another ablation 70.19% pass rate and 44.80% invalid. Solution aggregation added +3.51 METEOR, +4.50 BLEURT, +2.28% G-Helpfulness.
limits: Internal vendor data; text-similarity and stability measures.
agent_relevance: Evidence for tool loops with stored observations instead of reasoning from the alert text alone.

source: Shi 2023 vs Mirzadeh 2025 compared
finding: Distractor damage persists in newer models: GSM-IC (2023) and GSM-NoOp (2024) show the same effect, and more recent models declined more in the NoOp figure.
numbers: Figure 8a caption: more recent models experience a greater decline than older ones; o1-mini and o1-preview still drop significantly.
limits: Different benchmarks; comparison is by the authors' description.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the next model fixes it; keep the check in code.

source: Embers of Autoregression: two probabilities
finding: Both task probability and output probability change accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4 cipher 51% vs 13% by output probability.
limits: One task shown in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Rare faults need extra evidence because the model's prior favours the common answer.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) cause of selection bias
finding: Selection bias is prevalent across LLMs and option counts (two to five) and comes largely from a prior on label tokens.
numbers: Debiasing prior estimated on about 5% of test samples.
limits: Multiple-choice only.
agent_relevance: Option shuffling plus prior correction in code fits G5.
